prize_parts.citation: For the prediction of flat electronic bands at a magic twist angle in twisted bilayer graphene and the discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states, opening the field of moire quantum materials

statement.case_for: Twisted bilayer graphene is a rare case in which a simple, quantitative theory (the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model, which predicts the magic angle and the flat bands) preceded an experimental discovery (correlated insulators and superconductivity, 2018) that nobody expected from a carbon monolayer pair. It has since been independently reproduced by many groups and carried over to twisted multilayers, transition-metal dichalcogenide moire systems and fractional Chern insulator physics, so it is a new, tunable platform for correlated quantum matter rather than a single material. Theory and measurement agree on the central structure, which is what I look for, and the discovery again shows that quantum mechanics keeps surprising us, as 2D carbon did in 2010. It is also a physical discovery at the centre, not a method or a technology milestone.
statement.case_against: The field is only eight years old, and the microscopic mechanism of the superconductivity is still debated, so a citation must be worded around the observed phases and the flat-band prediction, not around an explanation. The credit is also messy: Yuan Cao, who led the 2018 experiments, and earlier moire band-structure theory (Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto, Shallcross and others) are outside the three names, and twist-angle disorder and sample variability still limit reproducibility at the quantitative level. If colleagues judge that the committee should wait for a settled mechanism, a more mature candidate such as B024 is the honest alternative.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the twisted-bilayer case only fourth, praising the elegance of the continuum model and the rapid reproduction, but he worries about the youth of the field, the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Yuan Cao and earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto.
responses.response: I share the worry about attribution and I think it is the main obstacle, but I read the maturity concern differently. What the prize would reward is the flat-band prediction and the observation of correlated and superconducting phases, both confirmed across many laboratories and moire platforms, and not a pairing theory. Cao's role is a real problem that the three-name limit forces on us, and I would rather the committee state openly that the experimental credit is a judgement about the group leader. On his own candidate, B051, I agree that 2D melting is elegant and was left out in 2016, but he himself notes that hard-disk simulations show first-order melting, so the clean statement of the discovery I would want in a citation is not yet obvious to me. It is outside my own area and I would like his reading of that point.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first as an experimentally original and conceptually surprising opening of moire quantum materials, reproduced by many groups within a decade, while flagging that the superconducting mechanism, junior-researcher credit and twist-angle disorder are unsettled. She puts NV centres (B046) second.
responses.response: I agree with her on the case and on the reproducibility record, and her point about sample-to-sample variability is one I would add to my own uncertainty list. I am more cautious than she is on B046: the single-NV optical detection and coherent control is a robust, widely reproduced result, but Lukin's later sensing work and the contributions of Awschalom, Hanson and others make the allocation crowded, and whether the discovery or the sensing application carries the prize is unsettled. I would keep it as an alternative, and her two-name version (Wrachtrup, Jelezko) is cleaner than the three-name one if we go that way.

responses.point: Kroll puts optical lattice clocks first: magic-wavelength trapping, uncertainties near 1e-18, relativity tests at the centimetre scale and an expected redefinition of the second, confirmed by many independent laboratories, with a clean two-name credit for Katori and Ye.
responses.response: This is the strongest case for maturity and attribution on the shortlist, and I would not oppose it. My reservation is not about quality but about scope: lattice clocks are a precision-instrument advance in a line already recognised in 2005 (frequency combs) and 2012 (single quantum systems), whereas I see the moire materials as a new regime of matter. I defer to him and Lindroth on the clock history and on how well the 1e-18 figures have been confirmed between laboratories, since I cannot check them from the condensed-matter side. I am willing to move to B024 if the committee finds the moire mechanism too immature.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube first as a concrete discovery from nature that opened neutrino astronomy, but notes that a single-name credit for Halzen is awkward for a collaboration-scale result and that the origin of most of the diffuse flux is unresolved.
responses.response: I defer to him on astroparticle physics, but his own attribution concern seems to me decisive against B019 as configured, since the supplied credit is one person and a collaboration of this size cannot be represented fairly that way. Our own caution about source identification is also fairly similar to his comment that the full astrophysical story is incomplete. On discovery value I am sympathetic: a new observational window is exactly the kind of verified discovery I want at the centre. If the committee can find a defensible multi-person credit for IceCube and AMANDA, I would reconsider.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as the architecture behind superconducting qubits and a natural continuation of the 2025 prize, while acknowledging a possible conflict from his own work, and that Girvin is excluded by the three-name limit.
responses.response: Circuit QED is an excellent, very mature result and I take his point that it is physically distinct from macroscopic quantum tunnelling. As the 2025 Chair I would nevertheless be reluctant to follow that prize so closely with another superconducting-circuit award, and the Girvin problem he identifies leaves the four-name credit unresolved. He is right to declare his proximity to the field, and I would ask that his view on B042 be weighted with that in mind.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the field as mature enough, given that the pairing mechanism of superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene is unresolved.
How to treat Yuan Cao and the earlier moire band-structure theorists who are outside the three credited names.
Whether twist-angle disorder and sample variability undermine the quantitative reproducibility of the correlated phases.
How well lattice-clock and IceCube priority histories hold up, which I cannot judge from my own field.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my provided profile for B020. My group works on DFT and magnetism, not moire materials, and I have no stated link to the credited names. I was Chair for the 2025 prize, which concerned superconducting circuits, and I should be mindful of that when weighing B042. Altermagnetism (B050), which is close to my own work, is not on the shortlist.
